The IMO's London headquarters
By Alexander Whiteman
26 November 2026
Surrendering the governance of maritime decarbonisation to fragmented and regional regulations could ultimately prove more expensive for the industry than a globally agreed framework, according to US Federal Maritime Commission chair Laura Di Bella.
Speaking to The Loadstar on the sidelines of the IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) in London this week, Ms Di Bella said the US was seeking a global agreement on the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework.
She added: “The regional schemes will ultimately be more costly than something done on a global level. It is harmful, and I believe it when industry says it’s going to be more costly.”
That belief stems from feedback the FMC has been gathering from industry participants, with the message very much stating that regulatory fragmentation would increase costs for shipping businesses.
Noting that the US was “approaching the negotiations in good faith” and wants to reach a global agreement, Ms Di Bella, nonetheless, warned disagreements over the proposed framework’s economic element remained a significant obstacle to reaching a consensus.
Under the proposal, ships that exceed fuel-intensity limits would be charged, with the money going into an emissions pricing and revenue-recycling mechanism that would reward zero-emission fuels.
However, the FMC chair said the mechanism was overshadowing discussions about greenhouse gas reductions, adding that “the economic element needs its own separate discussion, and then [so are] the GHG measures”.
For the US to accede the agreement, Ms Di Bella said, it would need to fit four principal requirements: no economic element; a fuel-agnostic approach; technology neutrality; and clarification over the treatment of emissions trading schemes (ETS).
On the latter, she said the US did not consider the prospect of receiving credits under a future scheme sufficient, calling for the removal of the existing ETS to avoid what she considers “double taxation”.
“We are continuing to engage with the other participants in an effort to bridge these differences, but we believe the economic element has come to dominate at the expense of the environment,” noted Ms Di Bella.
“We need negotiations to be focused on the environmental element. For this reason, if we are to see any progress, the ETS needs to go. It presents an opportunity to not only tax much, which is an issue we have, but then a second time. You cannot have both.”
